extracted.intended_audience: aspiring journalists and students of news writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative examples for reporting public events (fairs, openings, parades, dedications), emphasizing what to include and how style/tone shape a story. Uses sample dispatches to show factual reporting, human-interest detail, and contrasting tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare with reference to style and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Note — The next two stories, which describe a pageant parade, should be compared with reference to style and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paired examples to analyze differences in reporting voice, rhetorical choices, level of irony or seriousness, and how those choices affect reader impression (illustrated by the two automobile-pageant pieces from different papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid sensory description to convey atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: “The effect of the place is kaleidoscopic, or rather that of a talking moving picture run wild. It is a perfect jumble of color and sound.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sensory language (color, sound, motion) to recreate the scene for readers; exemplar passages describe bands, barkers, animals, horns and the overall discordant-but-pleasant impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include attendance figures and crowd description
rubrics_metrics.description: Report estimates and impressions: e.g., “a crowd variously estimated at between 60,000 and 80,000 persons,” and “the grand stands were jammed solid.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give numeric estimates where available and support with vivid adjectives or concrete evidence of density and enthusiasm to indicate scale and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name officials, speakers, and award winners
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify key persons and their roles — governors, mayors, speakers, judges, and winners (e.g., Gov. Samuel D. Felker; winners of the Lawson cup; judges’ lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List full names and titles; when relevant, indicate affiliations and actions (who spoke, who presented cups) to establish authority and factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report competitions/awards with technical/class details
rubrics_metrics.description: Give class specifications and results (examples: Lawson cup for gig horses not under 15.1 or over 15.3 hands; classes for park four-in-hands, tandems, Corinthian class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the contest class, eligibility or technical measurements, and the winner(s) to make results meaningful to knowledgeable readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply history and development context — e.g., the history of Washington Market, past reconstructions, prior visitors (Edward VII, Presidents Grant, Garfield, Arthur, Cleveland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed brief historical notes or institutional background to explain significance of the event or place and connect present actions to broader developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include direct quotes and full texts of important addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish speeches and letters as part of the report — shown by long quoted passages (Mayor Mitchel’s remarks; President Roosevelt’s and President Wilson’s letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When officials make formal statements of policy or congratulations, include verbatim extracts (or substantial paraphrase) so readers can judge substance and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe layout, exhibits, and notable devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail physical arrangements and exhibits: steel cages for fowl, centre duck pond tank, balcony for pigeons and pet stock, booths for incubators/ patent feeders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the venue for readers by describing major sections, unusual displays, and distinctive props or devices that characterize the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-interest anecdotes to enliven copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Include small, memorable stories — e.g., John, a rooster trained to grind bones who had an attack of stage-fright; trained hens operating a miniature turnstile that dispensed corn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add brief colorful anecdotes that illustrate the scene and engage readers emotionally while still supporting the factual account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance serious coverage with entertaining side attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover both the agricultural/technical exhibits and the Looney Lane amusements (wrestlers, diving girls, freaks), noting their character and costs (dime attractions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both the substantive, informative parts of an event and the popular/entertainment elements to reflect the event’s full character and audience appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail ceremonial/dedication program and participating organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: List participating societies, program order, and ceremonial participants for dedications (e.g., the Jeanne d’Arc unveiling listing twenty-one societies, speakers, invocation, anthems, and placement of presidential letter in the pedestal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dedications and formal ceremonies, provide the program itinerary and list institutional participants to document the civic and organizational dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret visual symbolism and artist intent in art reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer interpretive commentary about artworks and intentions: e.g., commentary on Anna Vaughn Hyatt’s depiction of Jeanne d’Arc as spiritual, sword held up to God, use of Tower of Rouen stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond reporting who and what to discuss artistic choices and symbolic meaning, citing artist background and materials when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide operational/logistical specifics for openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Give concrete operational details for inaugurations: times, first-train descriptions, routing under the river, ceremonial mechanisms (presidential telegraph key, button-pressing), and immediate follow-up (banquet at Sherry’s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey the mechanics of an opening (how it was done) to underline its novelty and practical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give material and financial specifics for public projects
rubrics_metrics.description: State construction costs, savings, materials and financial figures (e.g., the $60,000,000 tunnel; nearly $500,000 saved from a $3,000,000 appropriation; market finished in glass, marble, porcelain, enamel, nickel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hard numbers and material descriptions to show scale, investment, and the quality of public works or reconstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict social composition and contrasts in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray class and social variety: “the millionaire rubbed elbows with the farm boy,” comparisons of sartorial neatness vs. agrarian dress, young America vs. Old America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include observations about the crowd’s social makeup to convey atmosphere and civic reach of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report incidents, accidents, and near-misses
rubrics_metrics.description: Note mishaps and public-safety incidents: motorcycle nearly tipping, motorcycle colliding with an automobile, Ralph De Palma bumping a touring car and losing a mudguard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record any accidents or safety incidents to provide a complete, responsible account of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe spectacle: costumes, music, floats and theatrical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail parade spectacle — illuminated and decorated automobiles, musicians in war bonnets, floats like the Peace Float and Santa Claus Ship, novelty acts and themed costumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalog the visual and performative elements that make a parade or pageant visually and culturally interesting to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt tone appropriate to the paper’s approach (factual vs. ironic/columnistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast in practice: one paper’s piece is straightforward and celebratory, another is more sardonic/evocative (e.g., Herald’s straight parade report vs. World’s smoky, ironic rendering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate voice—straight news, feature, ironic commentary—consistent with the outlet’s style and the story’s purpose; be aware how tone shapes reader takeaways.
